a: For correction.
p: The heading's Greek eis elenchon means "for rebuke" or "to convict": the psalm owns that the exile was deserved.
b: Elenchos is a rebuke that proves someone wrong, the word of Proverbs for a parent's or teacher's correction. The psalm does exactly that: Israel was scattered "just as God had said" (9:2), and God is in the right (9:3). Like the other headings, this one may have been added by whoever gathered the eighteen psalms; Ryle and James suggest that the man who wrote the titles also added the two Selah marks, to make the book look more like the Psalter of David (see 17:31). The manuscript Swete calls i gives a longer title here that also has "for victory", the phrase of 8:0.
orig: εἰς ἔλεγχον (eis elenchon), 'for reproof'

a: taken away as captives to a foreign land
p: The words fit both the Babylonian exile and the captives Pompey took to Rome in 63 BC.
b: The psalm speaks the old language of the exile to Babylon (Deuteronomy 4:27; 2 Kings 17:6). Gray groups this verse with 2:3-15 and 8:24 as describing the captives "led away" by the invaders of his own day, that is, the Jews Pompey took west after 63 BC (see 17:14 and the notes on Psalm 8). So the poet reads a fresh disaster through Israel's oldest story of sin and exile. The manuscript Swete calls i has "Jerusalem" for "Israel".

a: the Lord who had set them free
p: The Greek lytroō is the ransom word of the Exodus.
b: Lytroō means to set free by paying a price, the Septuagint's verb for God bringing Israel out of Egypt (Deuteronomy 7:8). Luke's song of Zechariah uses the noun from the same root: God "has visited his people and worked their redemption" (Luke 1:68). The exiles turned away from the very God who had once bought them out of slavery.
orig: τοῦ λυτρωσαμένου αὐτούς (tou lytrōsamenou autous)

a: Israel was scattered among every nation
p: Moses warned that sin would bring scattering among the nations. The psalm says it came "just as God had said".
b: "The LORD will scatter you among the peoples. Only a few of you will be left among the nations where the LORD drives you" (Deuteronomy 4:27; compare Leviticus 26:33). The Greek diaspora, "scattering", became the name for Jews living outside the land; James writes "to the twelve tribes in the Dispersion" (James 1:1). Ryle and James join "among every nation" to the line before ("they were thrown out ... among every nation"); the sense is the same.
orig: ἡ διασπορὰ τοῦ Ἰσραήλ (hē diaspora tou Israēl)

a: you, God, would be shown to be in the right
p: The prayer of confession: the punishment proves God just. The same words open Baruch's and Daniel's prayers.
b: The Greek dikaiōthēs, "that you may be justified", is the language of Psalm 51: "So you are in the right when you speak, and clear when you pass judgment" (Psalm 51:4), which Paul quotes in Romans 3:4. Nehemiah's prayer says the same: "Yet you are in the right in all that has come on us" (Nehemiah 9:33; compare Daniel 9:7). The psalm does not ask why God allowed the disaster. It says the disaster shows that God keeps his word, and so his word of mercy can be trusted too (9:16-19).

a: your devout ones
p: Hosioi translates the Hebrew hasidim, the name the poets give themselves. The site keeps one rendering, "the devout".
b: Hosioi stands, Gray notes, for the Hebrew ḥasidim, "the loyal" or "the godly", as it does in the Greek Psalms. The same Hebrew stands behind the Hasideans who joined the Maccabees (1 Maccabees 2:42). Elsewhere the site renders the word by its setting: "holy ones" in Wisdom of Solomon, "holy sons" in Sirach 39:13, and "your loyal one" at Psalm 16:10 (from the Hebrew ḥasid). In this book it is a party name, the counterpart of "the sinners" (see 12:8), so it stays "the devout" every time. The "right deeds" (dikaiosynai, plural) are probably acts of mercy such as almsgiving, as Ryle and James argue.
orig: τῶν ὁσίων σου (tōn hosiōn sou)
r: Psalm 16:10; 1 Maccabees 2:42; Sirach 39:13; Wisdom of Solomon 18:9; 12:8

a: What we do lies in the choice and power of our own souls
t: "In the choice and power of our soul"
p: The Greek says our deeds lie "in the choice and power of our soul". This is the book's clearest word on free will.
b: Word for word: "our works (are) in choice and power of our soul, to do righteousness and unrighteousness in works of our hands." Ryle and James weighed a second way to divide it: "our works are by (God's) choice, and we have power to do right or wrong", a paradox like the saying in Mishnah Avot 3, "Everything is foreseen; and freewill is given" (Taylor's translation, which they quote). They note that eklogē in the New Testament always means God's choosing (Romans 9:11; 11:5). Gray rejected that division because the poem's rhythm will not bear it. The Plain English Translation keeps "soul", the word the verse turns on. Most readers take the plain sense: people choose, and God judges the choice (9:8-10).
orig: τὰ ἔργα ἡμῶν ἐν ἐκλογῇ καὶ ἐξουσίᾳ τῆς ψυχῆς ἡμῶν (ta erga hēmōn en eklogē kai exousia tēs psychēs hēmōn)

a: to do right or to do wrong
p: Josephus says the Pharisees held that doing right or not lies mostly with people, though fate helps. Scholars have long compared this verse.
b: Josephus wrote that the Pharisees "attribute everything to fate and to God", yet hold that doing what is right, or not, "lies for the most part with people", while fate also helps in each act (Jewish War 2.8.14, which Ryle and James quote in Greek; compare Jewish Antiquities 13.5.9 and 18.1.3). Gray found this "almost exactly paralleled" in the Psalms of Solomon and counted it among his reasons for calling the poets Pharisees. Sirach had said much the same a century earlier: God "left him in the hand of his own choice" (Sirach 15:14). The verse does not say that people save themselves; the same psalm rests its hope on God's choice of Israel and his mercy (9:16-19).

a: stores up life for himself with the Lord
p: The picture of storing up life with God comes back in Jesus' "pile up treasures for yourselves in heaven".
b: Thēsaurizei is "he stores up treasure". Ryle and James compare 4 Ezra's "treasure of works" and Jesus' saying: "Instead, pile up treasures for yourselves in heaven" (Matthew 6:20). They argue that for Jewish hearers the "right deeds" stored up were chiefly works of mercy, such as those listed in Matthew 25:35-46. Paul uses the same verb for the opposite: "You are treasuring up anger for yourself" (Romans 2:5).
orig: θησαυρίζει ζωὴν αὑτῷ (thēsaurizei zōēn hautō)

a: is himself to blame for his own ruin
p: The Greek is compressed: "he himself (is) cause of the soul in destruction."
b: Aitios means "responsible, to blame". The line stresses that ruin is the sinner's own doing, as the life of the righteous is the fruit of his doing. Gray renders the sense as forfeiting one's own life. The thought echoes Ezekiel: "The person who sins, that very person will die" (Ezekiel 18:4).
orig: αὐτὸς αἴτιος τῆς ψυχῆς ἐν ἀπωλείᾳ (autos aitios tēs psychēs en apōleia)

a: when it confesses and owns up to them
p: Exomologēsis and exagoria both mean confessing. Gray thinks one may be a doublet.
b: Exomologēsis is confession or open acknowledgment; exagoria, "speaking out", is rare (most manuscripts spell it exēgoria, Swete's note says). Gray suggests the second may be a doublet in the Greek. He also explains Swete's "in sins" as a misread Hebrew "from sins", the sense the Plain English Translation follows (see the variant). The thought is the Psalter's: the singer resolves to confess his rebellious acts to the LORD, and God lifts the guilt of his sin (Psalm 32:5). Compare 1 John 1:9.
orig: ἐν ἐξομολογήσει, ἐν ἐξαγορίαις (en exomologēsei, en exagoriais)

a: if not the sins of those who have sinned?
p: A striking line: forgiveness is precisely for those who have sinned. Here even the devout count themselves sinners.
b: In most of the book "the sinners" are the other party. Here the devout speak of their own sins (9:13, 9:15), and the poet makes a point that sounds close to Jesus: "I have not come to call righteous people. I have come to call sinners to repentance" (Luke 5:32). The difference is in 9:15: God's kindness is on those who sin "and then are sorry" (en metameleia, "in regret"). Ryle and James compare Mishnah Avot 4, "Repentance and good works are as a shield against punishment," and the joy over "one sinner who repents" (Luke 15:7).

a: not hold their sins against them
p: The verb euthynō usually means to straighten or to audit. Here God does not audit the sins of the righteous.
b: Euthynō is "to make straight", and in Athenian law "to call an official to account". Gray says it must mean "reprove" here, as the Syriac takes it. Compare Psalm 32:2: "Happy is the person the LORD does not charge with guilt." The righteous here are not sinless; they are people whose sins God chooses not to count.
orig: οὐκ εὐθυνεῖς (ouk euthyneis)

a: take your mercy away from us
t: Mercy, the Greek for loyal love
p: Eleos, "mercy", usually stands for the Hebrew hesed, the site's "loyal love".
b: Eleos is the Septuagint's usual word for Hebrew ḥesed, God's loyal, covenant love, which the site renders "loyal love" in the Hebrew Bible. The Psalms of Solomon were probably written in Hebrew (Gray calls this "now generally admitted"), so behind "mercy" here may stand that same word. The site renders the Greek "mercy" throughout this book, as in Luke 1:72 ("dealing in mercy with our fathers"). The word ends almost every psalm of this part (9:20; 10:9; 11:9; 13:11; 15:15; 16:15; 17:51; 18:10).
orig: ἔλεός σου (eleos sou)

a: our enemies will fall on us
p: The Greek says only "so that they do not attack us". The Plain English Translation names them as enemies.
b: The Greek hina mē epithōntai hēmin has no named subject: "so that they do not set upon us". Gray translates "lest they assail us" and notes that the Syriac reads "the peoples". The Plain English Translation supplies "our enemies", the sense the line needs; the psalm began with Israel scattered among the nations (9:1-2).
orig: ἵνα μὴ ἐπιθῶνται ἡμῖν (hina mē epithōntai hēmin)

a: you put your name on us
p: Being called by God's name meant belonging to him. Moses' blessing put the name on Israel.
b: With the blessing the priests "will put my name on the Israelites" (Numbers 6:27), and Jeremiah prays, "your name is spoken over us. Do not abandon us!" (Jeremiah 14:9). The last half-line is hard: all manuscripts have "you will not cease" (Swete's note shows the person of the verb varies), which Ryle and James say the verb can hardly mean. Von Gebhardt guessed "you will not reject us" and Ryle and James "you will abide among us" (both reported by Gray). The Plain English Translation keeps the Greek and takes it as "you will not stop" bearing your name on us.
orig: καὶ οὐ καταπαύσεις τὸν αἰῶνα (kai ou katapauseis ton aiōna)

a: You made a covenant with our ancestors about us
p: Exile does not cancel the covenant. Here the book agrees with the prophets and with Paul.
b: The psalm grounds its hope in God's choice of Abraham's offspring (9:17) and the covenant with the fathers. This matches the Hebrew Bible (Leviticus 26:44-45; Deuteronomy 4:31) and Paul's claim that "God does not take back his gifts and his call" (Romans 11:29). The pattern of the psalm, God choosing his people by grace and then judging each one by deeds (9:9-10), is close to what E. P. Sanders called "covenantal nomism" (see the topic page on the New Perspective).

a: forever and ever
p: The Greek eis ton aiōna kai eti, "forever and still more", is this book's refrain.
b: Eis ton aiōna kai eti translates the Hebrew le'olam va'ed, "forever and ever" (as in the Greek of Exodus 15:18). The same close ends Psalms 11 and 17 (11:9; 17:51). The "mercy" here is eleēmosynē, which in Tobit means alms; of God it means his merciful kindness.
orig: εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα καὶ ἔτι (eis ton aiōna kai eti)

a: hymns
p: Swete prints "In hymns", the reading of one manuscript. Most have "A hymn".
b: Swete's note shows that most manuscripts read hymnos, "A hymn", here, as in 14:0 and 16:0, and Gray reports "In hymns" from R alone (on matching Gray's letters to Swete's, see the variant). The phrase may echo the Hebrew binginot, "with stringed instruments", which Swete's Septuagint renders en hymnois in the headings of Psalms 6, 54, 55 and 67 (Psalm 4:0 has en psalmois there). Hymns in the Greek Psalter are songs of praise; this one praises God for discipline.
orig: Ἐν ὕμνοις (En hymnois)

a: Happy the man whom the Lord keeps in mind with a rebuke
p: The opening blessing takes up Job and Psalm 94: the one God corrects is fortunate.
b: "Think how fortunate a man is when God corrects him! So do not spurn the Almighty's discipline" (Job 5:17). "Happy is the one you train, Yah, the one you teach from your law" (Psalm 94:12). The psalm draws on Proverbs too: "For whoever the LORD loves, he rebukes" (Proverbs 3:12), where the Greek adds "and he whips every son he takes in", the line Hebrews quotes (Hebrews 12:6). Psalm 10 is a short sermon on that text.

a: whom he fences off from the evil road
p: The Greek ekyklōthē means "he was encircled" or "turned aside"; Gray follows the Syriac "restrained".
b: Ekyklōthē is "he was surrounded, led around". Ryle and James take it of God leading Israel "around" by a longer road (Exodus 13:18). Gray follows the Syriac, "whom he restrains", and reports a guess that the Greek was once ekōlythē, "he was hindered". The picture is of a shepherd or driver forcing an animal off a dangerous track with a whip.
orig: ἐκυκλώθη ἀπὸ ὁδοῦ πονηρᾶς (ekyklōthē apo hodou ponēras)

a: Whoever gets his back ready for the whip
p: The willing son offers his back. The Servant in Isaiah did the same.
b: "My back I gave to the floggers" (Isaiah 50:6). For the poet the willing acceptance of God's whip marks the righteous; the sinner resents it. Proverbs speaks of the rod for the back of the fool (Proverbs 10:13). The image is harsh to modern ears, but its point is trust: the whip is in a father's hand (13:8; 18:4). For the debate about the rod in raising children, see the topic page.

a: those who bear his discipline
p: Paideia is the training a father gives his son: teaching, correction, punishment.
b: Paideia is the word for raising and training a child, and in the Greek Bible for God's discipline (Proverbs 3:11; Hebrews 12:5-11). The site renders it "discipline", as in Sirach, and "instruction" where it means teaching. It is the key word of this part: 10:2-3; 13:6-9; 14:1; 16:11-13; 17:47; 18:4, 8. Gray notes that the devout accepted the troubles of their time as discipline from God, "which it was their duty to endure patiently".
orig: τοῖς ὑπομένουσιν παιδείαν (tois hypomenousin paideian)

a: the law of the everlasting covenant
p: Martyria, "testimony", is the Greek Bible's word for the law as God's witness.
b: "Testimony" (Hebrew edut, Greek martyria or martyrion) is a name for the law in the Psalms (Psalm 19:7; 119). Gray suggests the verse means that the witness to God's mercy is written in the law and is seen again whenever God "visits" people in their daily lives. The "everlasting covenant" is the covenant of Sinai and of the fathers (Leviticus 24:8; Psalm 105:10).
orig: ἡ μαρτυρία ἐν νόμῳ διαθήκης αἰωνίου (hē martyria en nomō diathēkēs aiōniou)

a: righteous and loyal
p: The word for "devout" is used here of God. As in Psalm 145:17, it means loyal.
b: The Greek hosios, which names the devout (9:6), is here said of the Lord. Gray explains that it stands for Hebrew ḥasid, "loyal, kind", as in Psalm 145:17: "In all his ways the LORD is righteous, and loyal in all his works," where the Greek has hosios. So the Plain English Translation says "loyal" of God, as the site's Psalm 145:17 does, and keeps "faithful" for pistos (14:1; 17:12). The devout are those who mirror God's own loyalty.
orig: δίκαιος καὶ ὅσιος (dikaios kai hosios)

a: the assembly of the people
p: The Greek has ekklēsia here and synagōgai in 10:8. Neither yet means a building.
b: Ekklēsia laou is "the gathering of the people", the Septuagint's term for Israel assembled for worship (Psalm 22:22; 149:1). In 10:8 "the assemblies (synagōgai) of Israel" may be local gatherings for prayer. Both words later became names for the Christian church and the Jewish synagogue, but here they mean groups of people gathered before God. Gray suggests that "the poor" in this verse are the devout themselves, in parallel with the first line.
orig: ἐν ἐκκλησίᾳ λαοῦ (en ekklēsia laou); συναγωγαὶ Ἰσραήλ (synagōgai Israēl)

a: lasting soundness of mind
p: Swete prints "for everlasting soundness of mind"; three manuscripts have "for everlasting gladness".
b: Sōphrosynē is self-control, sound mind, the Greek virtue of moderation; it is odd as the goal of salvation. Swete's note shows euphrosynē, "gladness", in the manuscripts he calls c, i and l (see the variant). Ryle and James print "gladness" and compare Isaiah 35:10: "lasting gladness will be on their heads". Gray renders "gladness" too. The Plain English Translation follows Swete's text; the oddness of "soundness of mind" here is one reason to think "gladness" may be original.
orig: εἰς σωφροσύνην αἰώνιον (eis sōphrosynēn aiōnion)

a: For waiting in hope.
p: Prosdokia is eager waiting for something about to happen. Luke uses the verb for those waiting for the kingdom.
b: Prosdokia is expectation, a looking-forward. Luke uses the verb prosdechomai for Simeon "looking forward to the comforting of Israel" (Luke 2:25) and Anna's hearers, "looking for Jerusalem to be redeemed" (Luke 2:38). Psalm 11 is the book's song of that waiting: it describes the return of the scattered as if it had already happened.
orig: εἰς προσδοκίαν (eis prosdokian)

a: Blow the trumpet in Zion
p: The opening is Joel 2:1 in the Greek, turned from alarm to joy. Isaiah's great trumpet gathers the scattered.
b: Swete's Septuagint of Joel 2:1 begins with the same words, salpisate salpingi en Seiōn, "Blow the trumpet in Zion" (the site's Joel 2:1, from the Hebrew, has "Blow the ram's horn in Zion"). Gray notes the psalm is based on Joel 2:1. In Joel the horn warns of judgment. Here it announces the homecoming of Isaiah 27:13: "On that day a great ram's horn will be blown, and the strays perishing in the land of Assyria ... will come." Jesus speaks of a "great trumpet" when his angels gather his chosen (Matthew 24:31).
orig: Σαλπίσατε ἐν Σιὼν ἐν σάλπιγγι (Salpisate en Siōn en salpingi)

a: the signal trumpet of the holy ones
p: The phrase is obscure: "the trumpet of signal of saints". It may call the holy ones together.
b: Salpinx sēmasias hagiōn is literally "trumpet of signal of holy (ones)". Gray takes it as the trumpet "to summon the saints" and reports Ryle and James's guess at the Hebrew behind it, "the holy trumpet of jubilee", the horn of Leviticus 25:9. In Numbers 10:5-10 the silver trumpets give signals to gather the people and break camp. Either way, the call is for God's own people to come home.
orig: ἐν σάλπιγγι σημασίας ἁγίων (en salpingi sēmasias hagiōn)

a: the voice of one who brings good news
p: The Greek euangelizomenou is the word of Isaiah 40:9 and 52:7, the root of "gospel".
b: "How lovely on the mountains are the feet of the one who brings good news" (Isaiah 52:7); "Climb a high mountain, Zion, you messenger of good news!" (Isaiah 40:9). The Greek of both has the verb used here, euangelizomai. The New Testament takes the same word for the news of Jesus (Romans 10:15 quotes Isaiah 52:7). Here the good news is that God has had mercy on Israel and has "visited" them.
orig: φωνὴν εὐαγγελιζομένου (phōnēn euangelizomenou)

a: visited them
p: Episkopē is a visit from God to judge or to save. Luke's Zechariah sings that God "has visited his people".
b: Episkopē means a visit, an inspection, and in the Greek Bible God's coming to deal with his people, for punishment or rescue (Genesis 50:24; Wisdom of Solomon 3:7). Luke uses the verb: "he has visited his people and worked their redemption" (Luke 1:68), and Jesus weeps over Jerusalem, "you did not recognize the season when you were visited" (Luke 19:44). The word returns in 10:5, 11:7 and 15:14.
orig: ἐν τῇ ἐπισκοπῇ αὐτῶν (en tē episkopē autōn)

a: Stand on a height, Jerusalem, and see your children
p: Baruch 4:36-5:9 has nearly the same pictures in the same order. Which borrowed from which is still debated.
b: Compare Baruch 5:5: "Get up, Jerusalem! Stand on the heights. Look around, toward the sunrise, and see your children gathered from where the sun goes down to where it comes up." Then Baruch's "every high mountain is to be brought low" (Baruch 5:7), the woods and "every sweet-smelling tree" giving shade (Baruch 5:8), and Jerusalem's new clothes (Baruch 5:1-2) answer 11:5-8. Gray reports that Ryle and James accept that Baruch depends on this psalm, while Viteau rejects that dependence; both judged the Greek older than AD 70. Gray points to Ryle and James for how both passages relate to Isaiah 40-66. The site's note on Baruch 5:5 leaves the direction open. See also the chapter page.

a: From the north they come
p: The four directions come from Isaiah and the Psalms: east, west, north, and the islands.
b: "Look, these will come from far away, and look, these from the north and from the west" (Isaiah 49:12); "gathering them from the lands, from sunrise and from sunset, from the north and from the sea" (Psalm 107:3). The "distant islands" are Isaiah's coastlands of the far west (Isaiah 60:9; 66:19). Ryle and James sort the Jewish texts on the return of the tribes, and place this psalm among those that copy the old prophets but add marvelous details. Jesus uses the same picture for Gentiles coming to the feast (Matthew 8:11).

a: He has brought high mountains down
p: Isaiah 40's leveled road for God becomes a road for the returning people.
b: "Each valley will rise up, and each mountain and hill sink low" (Isaiah 40:4). In Isaiah the road is for the LORD; here, as in Baruch 5:7, it is for Israel coming home. The Greek homalismos, "leveling", is the word Baruch uses. Luke quotes the Isaiah lines for John the Baptist's call to prepare the way (Luke 3:4-6).
orig: εἰς ὁμαλισμὸν (eis homalismon)

a: every sweet-smelling tree
p: Isaiah plants trees in the wilderness for the returning people. Only this psalm and Baruch speak of "trees of fragrance".
b: Ryle and James note that "tree of sweet savor" occurs only here and in Baruch 5:8, and compare the fragrant trees of 1 Enoch 24, a sign of God's blessing. Isaiah promises "In the wilderness I will put the cedar, the acacia, the myrtle and the olive" (Isaiah 41:19). Gray notes that the Syriac version has "seas" here for "sprang up", a play on words that some take as a trace of a Hebrew original, though he judged the Syriac a translation from the Greek.

a: Put on your glorious clothes, Jerusalem
p: Isaiah 52:1 calls Zion to put on beautiful clothes. Psalm 2 had stripped her.
b: "Put on your beautiful clothes, Jerusalem, the holy city!" (Isaiah 52:1). In Psalm 2 the city was stripped, a scene of Pompey's capture; Ryle and James note that Baruch seems to join the two pictures, mourning clothes off and glory on (Baruch 5:1-2). "The robe of your holiness" can also mean "the robe of your sanctuary": hagiasma elsewhere in this book is the Temple (see 2:3). Jerusalem's priestly robes would then be the Temple's restored worship. The brief term for hagiasma elsewhere is "the sanctuary", but here it stands as a genitive describing a robe, and Gray renders the phrase "thy holy robe", so the Plain English Translation gives "the robe of your holiness" and leaves the Temple sense to this note.
orig: τὴν στολὴν τοῦ ἁγιάσματός σου (tēn stolēn tou hagiasmatos sou)

a: On the tongue of law-breakers.
p: The Greek reads "in the tongue of law-breakers". Gray thinks a Hebrew "against" was misread.
b: En glōssē paranomōn is literally "in (the) tongue of law-breakers". Gray suggests that the Greek "in" renders a Hebrew preposition that also means "against", and that the heading was taken from the psalm's opening lines (12:1). Paranomos, "law-breaking", is the word the site renders "law-breaker" in this book; the plain anomos is "lawless".
orig: ἐν γλώσσῃ παρανόμων (en glōssē paranomōn)

a: whispering tongue
p: Psithyros is a whisperer, a slanderer who spreads talk in secret. Paul lists whisperers among sinners.
b: Psithyros means "whispering", and as a noun a gossip or slanderer. Sirach says, "Curse the whisperer and the one with two tongues" (Sirach 28:13). Paul puts whisperers in his list of sins: "They whisper behind backs" (Romans 1:29, psithyristas). The psalm's enemy is a man who ruins households by quiet slander. Ryle and James suppose he was a Sadducee who had informed against a leading Pharisee at court, but they add: "Further than this we cannot undertake to go."
orig: γλώσσης παρανόμου καὶ ψιθυροῦ (glōssēs paranomou kai psithyrou)

a: sets their beauty ablaze
p: 12:2-4 is damaged in the Greek. Gray calls the text and meaning "uncertain and obscure".
b: Swete's text runs, word for word, "as among a people fire kindling the beauty of it, the sojourning of him, to fill houses with lying tongue". The manuscripts differ: Gray gives from H "on a threshing-floor" for "among a people" and "stubble" for "beauty", readings Swete's note gives for the manuscripts he calls h, m and v ("stubble" also in p, which has a third form of the first word, allō, "another"). Gray leaves gaps in his translation and doubts that any reading or conjecture recovers the original. The Plain English Translation follows Swete's words and takes "his sojourning" (paroikia, 12:3) as "his presence among them". The sense is clear enough: slander spreads like fire (James 3:6).
orig: ὥσπερ ἐν λαῷ πῦρ ἀνάπτον καλλονὴν αὐτοῦ (hōsper en laō pyr anapton kallonēn autou)

a: cuts down trees of gladness
p: The slanderer cuts down "trees of gladness". Gray suggests the trees are the devout themselves.
b: Gray asks whether the "trees of gladness" stand for the saints, comparing 14:2, where "the trees of life" are the Lord's devout. Psalm 1 makes the righteous a tree planted by water (Psalm 1:3), and Isaiah calls Zion's mourners "Oaks of Righteousness, the LORD's planting" (Isaiah 61:3). Cutting them down would mean ruining the good people of a town.

a: the houses of law-breakers
p: The Greek has "law-breaking houses". Gray thinks the adjective was copied by mistake from the line before.
b: Swete's text reads oikous paranomous, "law-breaking houses", and the Plain English Translation keeps it as "the houses of law-breakers". Gray translates only "households": the adjective stands in different places in different manuscripts, and he thinks it "probably a dittograph from the previous line", that is, copied by mistake from 12:3. If it is original, he says, the slanderer will not hesitate to set people of his own party against each other.
orig: συνχέαι οἴκους παρανόμους (syncheai oikous paranomous)

a: May the bones of whisperers be scattered
p: To have one's bones scattered was the curse of the unburied enemy.
b: "For God has scattered the bones of your besieger" (Psalm 53:5). Bones left unburied and scattered were a sign of utter defeat and God's judgment (Ezekiel 6:5; Jeremiah 8:1-2). The poet asks that the slanderers' power be broken and that they be kept "far from those who fear the Lord".

a: the quiet soul
p: The devout here are the quiet, peacemakers at home. Gray called them "political quietists".
b: Hēsychios is quiet, calm, not quarrelsome. Gray drew from this verse that the devout were "political quietists", who accepted the present distress as God's discipline rather than taking up arms. Ryle and James, writing of Psalm 10, contrast them with the Zealots, who were not "those who bear discipline". The New Testament praises the same temper: "a gentle and calm spirit" (1 Peter 3:4), and "Blessed are the peacemakers" (Matthew 5:9).
orig: ψυχὴν ἡσύχιον (psychēn hēsychion)

a: Israel his servant
p: Pais, "servant" or "child", is the word of Isaiah's Servant songs.
b: Pais can mean servant or child. Isaiah calls Israel "my servant" (Isaiah 41:8, Greek pais), and Mary's song says God "has taken hold of Israel, his servant, to help him" (Luke 1:54). The site renders pais "servant" (see 17:23, where Israel is again God's servant). The manuscript Swete calls i has "his servants".
orig: Ἰσραὴλ παῖδα αὐτοῦ (Israēl paida autou)

a: May the sinners be destroyed
p: In this book "the sinners" are a party as much as a moral class: Gray thought them the Sadducees and the ruling house.
b: Hoi hamartōloi appear in almost every psalm, set against "the devout". Gray says the book divides Israel into two parties and warns that "we are dealing with a strongly partisan work". He identified the sinners as the wealthy ruling party who served the later Hasmonean kings, and the righteous with the Pharisees; others are less sure (see the book's opening pages). Sometimes "sinners" are Gentiles (17:25-27), as in Paul's "sinners from the Gentiles" (Galatians 2:15). The devout "inherit the promises": the land and the life to come.
orig: οἱ ἁμαρτωλοί (hoi hamartōloi)

a: from famine and from the death that sinners die
p: Gray reads this as the kind of death sinners die: early, violent, or with no life after it.
b: Gray explains "the death of sinners" as premature or violent death, or "death beyond which lies no eternal life", the kind of death sinners die, and compares Balaam's wish in Numbers 23:10, "May I die the way the upright die", which he cites as "the death of the righteous". He also offers another explanation: the Greek may come from a wrong division of the Hebrew, which would then have read "from famine and pestilence; as for sinners, noisome beasts". In that case the passage refers to the four judgments of Ezekiel 14:21: "sword and famine and wild animals and plague." Sword, famine, wild beasts and death all appear in 13:2-3.
orig: ἀπὸ λιμοῦ καὶ θανάτου ἁμαρτωλῶν (apo limou kai thanatou hamartōlōn)

a: with their back teeth they crushed their bones
p: Mylai means both "molars" and "millstones". The Syriac took it the wrong way.
b: Mylē is a mill, and in the plural the molar teeth. Gray points out that the Syriac version rendered it "with millstones", which shows that the Syriac was translated from the Greek, since in Hebrew the two words would look nothing alike. The beasts may be real (Ezekiel 14:21) or the nations pictured as beasts (Daniel 7).
orig: ἐν ταῖς μύλαις (en tais mylais)

a: ungodly man
p: Every manuscript has "the ungodly". Many scholars think the sense needs "the righteous".
b: Gray calls "the righteous" "a conjectural substitute, which the context demands", adopted by Wellhausen, von Gebhardt and Kittel, for "the impious", "the reading of all MSS." of the Greek and the Syriac. On that reading it is the righteous man who trembles at his own faults, afraid to be swept away with the sinners, which fits 13:5-7. Gray sends readers to Ryle and James for "a defence of the text" of the Greek. The Plain English Translation follows the manuscripts (see the variant).
orig: ἐταράχθη ὁ ἀσεβὴς (etarachthē ho asebēs)

a: for what they did without knowing
p: The law gives offerings for sins done without knowing. The devout worry about those.
b: En agnoia, "in ignorance", recalls the law's offerings for one who sins "without meaning to" (Leviticus 4:2; Numbers 15:27-29). Gray counts "scrupulous anxiety about sins done in ignorance" among the marks of the devout. Hebrews says the high priest offered "for the sins the people committed in ignorance" (Hebrews 9:7), and 18:5 below speaks of the folly that comes "from not knowing".
orig: ἐν ἀγνοίᾳ (en agnoia)

a: The righteous is disciplined in private
p: En peristolē is unclear: "secretly", "sparingly", or "gently".
b: Peristolē is a wrapping or covering. Gray offers "Secretly" or "Sparingly" and calls the meaning uncertain, sending readers to Ryle and James. The point of the line is clear: God does not shame the righteous in public, "so that the sinner will not gloat".
orig: ἐν περιστολῇ (en peristolē)

a: like a son he loves
p: God trains the righteous as a father trains a dear son, as Deuteronomy and Proverbs say.
b: "So know in your heart that the LORD your God trains you the way a man trains his son" (Deuteronomy 8:5). "For whoever the LORD loves, he rebukes, the way a father treats the son he takes pleasure in" (Proverbs 3:12). Israel is God's "firstborn" (Exodus 4:22), the image of 18:4. Hebrews makes the same argument for Christians: "God is dealing with you as his sons" (Hebrews 12:7).

a: For the life of the righteous lasts forever
p: Life without end for the righteous, and destruction with no memory for sinners (13:10).
b: The book hopes for more than long life: the righteous live "forever" (13:9; 14:2; 15:15), and Psalm 3 says that those who fear the Lord will rise to life (see the notes on Psalm 3). Daniel 12:2 also speaks of "life without end". Where Daniel says some wake "to shame, to a horror without end", this book's sinners are "carried off to destruction" and forgotten (13:10; compare 15:13). It agrees with Daniel on the life of the righteous, and it is quieter than the New Testament on the fate of the wicked, which John 5:28-29 and Acts 24:15 describe as a resurrection to judgment.

a: so that we would live
p: The law was given "for our life", as Leviticus says: the one who does it will live.
b: "Keep my rules and my rulings. If a human being does them, he will live by them" (Leviticus 18:5). Gray notes that the Greek is "unto our life". In 14:2 "by it" may mean by the law, or "in him", the Lord (Gray gives both). Paul quotes Leviticus 18:5 twice to contrast the law with faith (Romans 10:5; Galatians 3:12). For this poet the law is God's gift of life to Israel, and "bearing his discipline" is part of keeping it.

a: the Lord's paradise, the trees of life
p: The devout are God's paradise and his trees of life, planted forever.
b: Paradeisos is a Persian word for a walled park, the Greek Bible's word for the garden of Eden (Genesis 2:8). The "tree of life" stood in its middle (Genesis 2:9). Here the devout themselves are the trees of God's garden, like the tree by the water in Psalm 1:3 and "the LORD's planting" in Isaiah 61:3. The New Testament promises the faithful "to eat from the tree of life, which is in the paradise of God" (Revelation 2:7).
orig: ὁ παράδεισος τοῦ κυρίου, τὰ ξύλα τῆς ζωῆς (ho paradeisos tou kyriou, ta xyla tēs zōēs)
r: Genesis 2:8-9; Psalm 1:3; Isaiah 61:3; Revelation 2:7; Revelation 22:2; Luke 23:43

a: all the days of heaven
p: "All the days of heaven" is a Hebrew way to say forever.
b: Gray calls "all the days of heaven" a synonym for "for ever" and compares Psalm 89:29 ("his throne for as many days as the heavens have") and Job 14:12. "God's share" is the language of Deuteronomy 32:9: "For the LORD's own share is his people; Jacob is the inheritance measured out for him."

a: Their longing is for a little rot
p: The Greek is odd: their desire is "in littleness of decay", that is, in brief, rotten pleasure.
b: En mikrotēti saprias is word for word "in smallness of rottenness". Gray renders "fleeting corruption", noting that "fleeting" stands for "littleness of". The "day" they loved (14:4) is the short life of pleasure, against the devout who live "forever". Sapria, rot, returns in 16:14.
orig: ἐν μικρότητι σαπρίας (en mikrotēti saprias)

a: the hidden rooms of the heart
p: Tameia are inner rooms or storerooms. God knows them before anything happens.
b: Tameia kardias are the inner storerooms of the heart. Proverbs says the LORD's lamp goes "searching through every inner room of the belly" (Proverbs 20:27). God knows people's ways "before anything happens", a strong statement of his foreknowledge beside the free choice of 9:7. Compare Psalm 139:1-4 and Jesus' "go into the storeroom of your house" (tameion, Matthew 6:6).
orig: ταμεῖα καρδίας (tameia kardias)

a: their inheritance is Hades, darkness and destruction
p: The sinners inherit Hades; the devout inherit life. A sharper split than most of the Hebrew Bible.
b: Hadēs is the Greek Bible's word for Sheol, the place of the dead. In most of the Hebrew Bible all the dead go there (Psalm 89:48). Here it has become the sinners' lot, "Hades, darkness and destruction", while the devout "inherit life" (compare 15:11). Gray: for the sinners "all that awaits them after death is destruction in Sheol". This goes beyond most of the Hebrew Bible and stands near Daniel 12:2 and Jesus' story of the rich man in Hades (Luke 16:23).
orig: ἡ κληρονομία αὐτῶν ᾅδης καὶ σκότος καὶ ἀπώλεια (hē klēronomia autōn hadēs kai skotos kai apōleia)

a: on the day when the righteous receive mercy
p: Literally "the day of mercy of the righteous". Psalm 18 calls it "the day of mercy".
b: The "day of mercy" (18:6, 18:10) is the coming day when God judges and rescues. Ryle and James say the "day of mercy" of 18:6 is this same day, seen from the side of those who receive mercy. Compare Paul: "Look, now is the day of salvation!" (2 Corinthians 6:2).
orig: ἐν ἡμέρᾳ ἐλέους δικαίων (en hēmera eleous dikaiōn)

a: A new psalm
p: The Psalter's "new song". Most manuscripts read "a new psalm"; one has "a psalm and praise".
b: "Sing a new song to the LORD; sing to the LORD, all the earth" (Psalm 96:1). Gray reports "A new psalm" from most manuscripts and the Syriac, and "a psalm and praise" from H, which Swete's note gives for manuscripts h, m, p and v (the Greek kainon and kai ainon differ by one space). A new song is the song of a fresh rescue (15:1). Revelation hears the redeemed sing "a new song" (Revelation 5:9).
orig: ψαλμὸν καινὸν (psalmon kainon)

a: fruit of the lips
p: Praise is a sacrifice: "the fruit of lips", as in Hosea 14:2 and Hebrews 13:15.
b: Hosea calls Israel to "pay you the bulls of our lips" (Hosea 14:2), where the Greek reads "the fruit of our lips". Hebrews takes up the Greek: "let us keep bringing up to God a sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that confess his name" (Hebrews 13:15). The psalm calls praise a "first harvest" (aparchē), the firstfruits offered at the Temple. Its poets lived after Pompey's soldiers had defiled the altar (2:2), and the praise of a righteous heart is their offering.
orig: καρπὸν χειλέων (karpon cheileōn); ἀπαρχὴν χειλέων (aparchēn cheileōn)

a: God's sign is on the righteous
p: God marks the righteous to save them, as Ezekiel's man with the writing case marked the faithful in Jerusalem.
b: "Make a mark on the foreheads of the people who sigh and groan over all the abhorrent things done in it" (Ezekiel 9:4); the destroyers then spare those marked. The blood on the doors at Passover was "a sign" (Exodus 12:13). Ryle and James compare Ezekiel 9:4 and the sign God set on Cain (Genesis 4:15). Revelation takes up Ezekiel: the angels wait "until we have sealed the slaves of our God on their foreheads" (Revelation 7:3). The Greek sēmeion is a sign or mark.
orig: τὸ σημεῖον τοῦ θεοῦ (to sēmeion tou theou)

a: Famine and sword and death
p: Famine, sword and death are the covenant curses. They are pictured as hunters that chase only the sinners.
b: Sword, famine and plague are the curses of Leviticus 26:25-26 and Jeremiah's repeated triad (Jeremiah 14:12). Gray notes that "death" here means pestilence, and that in 15:9 "they" are these plagues: they flee from the devout but hunt down the sinners. Psalm 91 promises the same: "Though a thousand drop at your side ... it will not reach you" (Psalm 91:7).

a: like people chased in war
p: These words are a conjecture. The manuscripts have "pursued from famine" or "by famine".
b: Swete prints diōkomenoi polemou, "pursued (in) war", which his note marks as von Gebhardt's conjecture. Gray records the manuscripts: diōkomenoi, "pursued" (J), or the genitive diōkomenou, "of one pursued" (R L C H), then "from famine" (R J) or "famine" (L C H), readings that "yield no tolerable sense". The Syriac has "as death flees from life". So the plagues flee "like people chased in war", a picture that fits the next lines. The Plain English Translation follows Swete (see the variant).
orig: ὡς διωκόμενοι πολέμου (hōs diōkomenoi polemou)

a: the sign of destruction is on their foreheads
p: The righteous bear God's sign; the sinners bear a mark of destruction on their foreheads.
b: Here the book has two marks, as Revelation does: God's seal on the foreheads of his servants (Revelation 7:3; 9:4) and the beast's mark "on the forehead or on the hand" of those who worship it (Revelation 14:9). In Ezekiel 9:4 only the faithful are marked. The psalm agrees with Ezekiel and Revelation that God knows and protects his own in the judgment. It does not say who puts the mark on the sinners; in Revelation the beast does (Revelation 13:16).

a: all the way down to Hades
p: Their lawless deeds hunt them down to Hades. Most manuscripts have "to Hades below"; one has "to the lowest".
b: Heōs hadou katō, "to Hades below". Swete's note shows that the manuscript he calls i reads "to the lowest" (katōtatou). The sins themselves become pursuers, as in Numbers 32:23: "Know this: your sin will find you." On Hades see the note at 14:6.
orig: ἕως ᾅδου κάτω (heōs hadou katō)

a: on the day of the Lord's judgment
t: The day of the Lord's judgment
p: The day of judgment as one coming day: the prophets' "day of the LORD".
b: Ryle and James note that "the day of judgment" for the final judgment appears in Judith 16:17 and often in the New Testament (Matthew 10:15; 2 Peter 3:7). The prophets called it "the day of the LORD" (Joel 2:1; Amos 5:18). In 15:14 it is the day "when God visits the earth", the same visiting word as 11:2. The manuscripts Swete calls h, m, p and v add a line after 15:14 and lack the last line of 15:15 (see the variants).

a: I nearly slipped
p: The psalm borrows the words of Psalm 73:2 in its Greek form: "nearly" and "almost poured out".
b: In the Greek Psalm 73:2 (72:2 in the Greek numbering) the steps of the singer were "almost" shaken and "nearly poured out" (par' oligon exechythē), the very words of 16:1-2. The site's Psalm 73:2, from the Hebrew, reads: "But me, my feet had almost turned aside; my steps had all but slid out from under me." In both, a believer nearly lost his footing, and God held him.
orig: παρὰ μικρὸν ὠλίσθησα (para mikron ōlisthēsa); παρ᾽ ὀλίγον ἐξεχύθη (par' oligon exechythē)

a: heavy with sleep
p: Swete prints "falling of sleep"; five manuscripts have "corruption of sleep". Gray reads "the pit".
b: Swete prints en kataphora hypnou, "in a sinking-down of sleep", the reading Gray gives from R and L. Gray reports "in corruption of sleep" (kataphthora) from J, C and H (Swete's note gives it to c, i, l, m and v; see the variant), and argues that kataphthora was the original Greek, standing for Hebrew shachat, "the pit", as in the Greek of Psalm 49:9; "of sleep" he thinks a misplaced gloss. The image is spiritual drowsiness: the singer was drifting from God as a sleeper drifts toward death (16:2; compare Romans 13:11).
orig: ἐν καταφορᾷ ὕπνου (en kataphora hypnou)

a: close to the gates of Hades
p: The gates of Hades are the gates of death. Jesus promises they will not prevail against his church.
b: The psalmist calls God the one "who raise me from the gates of death" (Psalm 9:13); Hezekiah feared, "I must walk into the gates of Sheol" (Isaiah 38:10). Of his church Jesus says, "the gates of Hades will not be stronger than it" (Matthew 16:18). Here the singer stood at those gates "with the sinner", in danger of sharing his end.

a: He jabbed me as a horse is jabbed with a goad
p: A goad is a pointed stick for driving animals. God jabbed the drowsy singer awake.
b: The Greek is "like the goad of a horse". The risen Jesus tells Paul, "Kicking against the goads is hard on you" (Acts 26:14), and Ecclesiastes says, "The words of the wise are like ox goads" (Ecclesiastes 12:11). "To keep me awake for him" is epi tēn grēgorēsin autou, "toward his watchfulness"; Ryle and James render "that I might watch unto him", and Gray "that I might serve Him". Swete's note shows that the manuscript he calls i lacks 16:4 and the first half of 16:5.
orig: ὡς κέντρον ἵππου (hōs kentron hippou); ἐπὶ τὴν γρηγόρησιν αὐτοῦ (epi tēn grēgorēsin autou)

a: every evil woman who trips up a fool
p: The prayer asks protection from the woman Proverbs warns about.
b: "Honey drips from the strange woman's lips, and her palate is smoother than oil" (Proverbs 5:3); Proverbs 7 tells how a young man goes after her "as an ox walks to the slaughter" (Proverbs 7:22). Gray counts "abstention (xvi. 7 f.) from the sexual sins which so offended them in their opponents" among the marks of the devout (compare 2:13-15; 8:9). The verb skandalizō is "to trip up, to make stumble", the New Testament's word for causing someone to sin (Matthew 18:6).
orig: γυναικὸς πονηρᾶς σκανδαλιζούσης ἄφρονα (gynaikos ponēras skandalizousēs aphrona)

a: or anything that comes from sin that does no good
p: The Greek "of everything lying under from sin unprofitable" is unclear.
b: Kai pantos hypokeimenou apo hamartias anōphelous is hard to construe. Gray reports Ryle and James's guess pan to synkeimenon, "nor aught that consists in sinful vanity". The Plain English Translation takes it as a second thing that might deceive: anything at all that arises from useless sin.
orig: καὶ παντὸς ὑποκειμένου ἀπὸ ἁμαρτίας ἀνωφελοῦς (kai pantos hypokeimenou apo hamartias anōphelous)

a: in your place
t: In your place, or before you?
p: Swete prints "in your place"; most manuscripts have "in your pattern". Gray thinks the original was "before you".
b: Gray reports "in your place" (en topō sou) from J alone, and "in your pattern" (en typō sou) from all the other Greek manuscripts, and he thinks both came from an original enōpion sou, "before you", which the Syriac reflects. Swete prints topō. The prayer asks God to keep the singer's work straight where God is: the Temple, or simply in his presence (Psalm 90:17).
orig: ἐν τόπῳ σου (en topō sou)

a: if I sin while you discipline me to bring me back
p: The singer asks for patience under discipline, because God's discipline aims at return.
b: Eis epistrophēn, "for turning back", names the goal of discipline: repentance. The singer does not ask to escape correction, only to bear it without "grumbling and faint-heartedness" (compare Numbers 14:27; Philippians 2:14). Hebrews says the same: discipline "hands back a peaceful fruit, righteousness, to those who have been put through their training by it" (Hebrews 12:11). Swete's note shows that the manuscript he calls l lacks the first line of the verse.
orig: ἐν τῷ σε παιδεύειν εἰς ἐπιστροφήν (en tō se paideuein eis epistrophēn)

a: what I have been given will be enough for me
p: The prayer for contentment matches Proverbs 30:8 and Paul's "I have learned to be content".
b: "Do not give me poverty or riches. Feed me with the bread that is my share" (Proverbs 30:8). Paul: "Whatever situation I am in, I have learned to be content with it" (Philippians 4:11). The verb arkeō, "be enough", is the word of 2 Corinthians 12:9: "My grace is enough for you." Gray took 16:12-14 as a sign that many of the devout were poor (compare 15:2; 18:3).
orig: ἀρκέσει μοι τὸ δοθέν (arkesei moi to dothen)

a: when a soul is corrected by the hand of its own decay?
p: Gray calls the sense "obscure". "Decay" (sapria) may mean the frailty of the body.
b: Word for word: "in the being-rebuked a soul in hand of rottenness of it". Gray links sapria with 14:4 and calls the sense obscure. The next line makes the thought plain enough: God tests a person "in his body" (Greek sarx, flesh) and by poverty. Compare Job, tested in his body (Job 2:5), and Paul's "thorn in the flesh" (2 Corinthians 12:7).
orig: ἐν χειρὶ σαπρίας αὐτοῦ (en cheiri saprias autou)

a: For the king.
p: Tō basilei can mean "to the king" or "for the king". The psalm is about God the King and his chosen king.
b: The dative tō basilei may dedicate the psalm "to the King" (God, as in 17:1 and 17:51) or mark it "for the king", the son of David it prays for (17:23). It is the only heading in the book with this phrase. The site renders tō Salōmōn "Of Solomon" (as Psalm 72:0), and the same ambiguity attaches to the king here.
orig: τῷ βασιλεῖ (tō basilei)

a: Lord, you are our King forever and ever
p: The psalm opens and closes on God's kingship. The coming king will rule under God, not instead of him.
b: The frame of 17:1 and 17:51 ("The Lord himself is our King forever and ever") is the creed of the Psalter: "The LORD is king always and forever" (Psalm 10:16; compare Psalm 145:13; Exodus 15:18). Inside the frame stands the human king (17:23-46), whose own King is the Lord (17:38). This is the book's answer to the Hasmonean kings, and later to Pompey and Rome: kingship belongs to God, and he gives it to whom he promised.

a: so does the hope placed in him
p: Hope set on a man lasts only as long as he does. Hope in God lasts forever (17:3).
b: Gray: "Transitory as is man's life, so transitory is the hope which one man places in another; but ... the hope placed in God is eternal." Compare Psalm 146:3-4: "Do not rely on nobles ... His breath leaves, he goes back to his ground." After the fall of the Hasmonean kings and the coming of Pompey, the point was sharp.

a: the kingdom of our God
p: "The kingdom of our God" is close to the phrase Jesus made central. Most manuscripts add "in judgment".
b: Hē basileia tou theou hēmōn, "the kingdom of our God": compare "Your kingdom is a kingdom for all ages" (Psalm 145:13) and Daniel 2:44. Jesus' first preaching is "the kingdom of God has drawn near" (Mark 1:15). Swete follows the manuscript he calls r here; the others add "in judgment" (see the variant).
orig: ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ ἡμῶν (hē basileia tou theou hēmōn)

a: you swore to him about his offspring forever
p: The psalm rests its hope on God's oath to David in 2 Samuel 7 and Psalm 89.
b: "Your house and your kingdom will be made secure forever in front of you. Your throne will stand firm for all time" (2 Samuel 7:16). "I have made a covenant with the one I chose; I have taken an oath to David, my servant" (Psalm 89:3). The Greek of Psalm 89:3 (88:4 in the Greek) has ōmosa Daueid, "I swore to David", the verb used here. Peter appeals to the same oath for Jesus (Acts 2:30).
orig: σὺ ὤμοσας αὐτῷ περὶ τοῦ σπέρματος (sy ōmosas autō peri tou spermatos)

a: sinners rose up against us
t: Who were the sinners who took the throne?
p: Most scholars take them to be the Hasmonean priest-kings, who were not of David's line.
b: Gray notes that the sinners here are "Jews, not foreigners". He reads 17:7-8 as the charge that they "had set up a non-Davidic monarchy", and so identifies them with "the adherents of the later Hasmoneans who from Aristobulus I (104 B.C.) and onwards claimed the title of king" until Pompey deposed Aristobulus II in 63 BC. The Hasmoneans were priests of the family of Mattathias (1 Maccabees 2:1), not sons of David. "What you had not promised them" is the throne that God promised only to David's house (17:5). Frankenberg, Gray reports, explained the verse of the Babylonian assault on Jerusalem, and Ryle and James took "us" to be the priests. See also the topic page on the Hasmoneans.

a: a royal house to match their high rank
p: The Greek antì hypsous autōn is hard: "in place of their height" or "to suit their pride".
b: Basileion anti hypsous autōn is word for word "a kingdom in place of their height". It may mean that they made themselves kings "to match" their own exalted rank as high priests, or "in place of" the true glory God had given them, the priesthood. Gray renders "a worldly monarchy in place of that which was their excellency". The poets object to priests who took the crown.
orig: ἔθεντο βασίλειον ἀντὶ ὕψους αὐτῶν (ethento basileion anti hypsous autōn)

a: in the arrogance of their exchange
p: Swete's allagmatos means "exchange"; four manuscripts have alalagmatos, "war cry".
b: Allagma is a thing given in exchange. If original, the arrogance was in their swap: their own royal house in place of David's. Swete's note gives alalagmatos, "shouting" or "war cry", from the manuscripts he calls h, m, p and v, which Gray follows ("tumultuous arrogance"). See the variant.
orig: ἐν ὑπερηφανίᾳ ἀλλάγματος (en hyperēphania allagmatos)

a: a man foreign to our race
p: Most scholars identify the foreign man with Pompey, who ended the Hasmonean kingdom in 63 BC.
b: Gray: "A man that was alien to our race" is Pompey, who "came from the West, and thither he carried back captive Aristobulus and his children." Gray also reports Frankenberg's very different view, that this man is not Pompey nor Antiochus but the Messiah, which he did not accept. The poet sees the foreign conqueror as God's tool to punish the usurpers, as Isaiah saw Assyria (Isaiah 10:5-6). On Pompey's capture of Jerusalem see Psalms 2 and 8 and their notes.
orig: ἄνθρωπον ἀλλότριον γένους ἡμῶν (anthrōpon allotrion genous hēmōn)

a: He hunted down their offspring and did not let one of them go
p: The verse pictures the ruling family hunted down. Gray links "take their offspring away" (17:8) to the Romans' capture of Aristobulus.
b: Gray takes "take their offspring away from the earth" (17:8) as "a specific allusion to Pompey's carrying captive to Rome Aristobulus and his children" (see 17:14). The words sound like the end of the whole house; the poet speaks as the prophets did of fallen dynasties (1 Kings 14:10). Swete's note shows that most manuscripts begin this verse with "according to their deeds" (Gray calls it a copying slip from 17:10), and that h, m, p and v lack the first "not" (see the variant).

a: The lawless one
t: The lawless one or the wind?
p: Three manuscripts have anomos, "the lawless one"; four have anemos, "the wind".
b: Swete prints ho anomos, "the lawless one", from the manuscripts he calls i, l and r; his note gives ho anemos, "the wind", from h, m, p and v. The two Greek words differ by one letter. A scorching wind is a biblical picture of an invader (Jeremiah 4:11-12), but Gray, who follows "the lawless one", says the singular in 17:13-16 is used collectively of the enemy "or specifically of their leader (Pompey)". Paul's "lawless one" (2 Thessalonians 2:8) is a later figure, but the same word. See the variant.
orig: ὁ ἄνομος (ho anomos)

a: In anger, in his splendor
p: The Greek says "in anger of his beauty". Gray thinks a Hebrew word for "heat" was misread.
b: En orgē kallous autou is literally "in anger of his beauty", an odd phrase. Gray thinks a Hebrew word for "his anger" was misread as "his beauty", renders "In the heat of His anger", and says the pronouns probably refer to God. Others take the subject to be the conqueror in his proud splendor. The Plain English Translation keeps both words of the Greek.
orig: ἐν ὀργῇ κάλλους αὐτοῦ (en orgē kallous autou)

a: he sent them away as far as the west
p: Pompey took Aristobulus II and his children to Rome. The psalm calls Rome "the west".
b: Gray: Pompey "came from the West, and thither he carried back captive Aristobulus and his children". Gray counts this among the details that fit Pompey and no other known conqueror, and cites Josephus for the captives (Jewish Antiquities 14.4.5; 14.5.4; 14.6.1; Jewish War 1.7.7; 1.8.6). "The rulers of the land were made a laughingstock" may recall the captive princes led in Pompey's triumph at Rome; the psalm does not say so, and the site's notes on Psalms 2 and 8 discuss the history.

a: what the nations do for their gods in their cities
p: Gray thinks 17:16 is incomplete. Frankenberg read it of Antiochus IV, Gray of Pompey.
b: Swete's text is "and all things whatever he did in Jerusalem, as also the nations in the cities the gods of them". Gray explains at length that R's reading tous theous (Swete's text, from r) is probably older than tois theois in the rest, and that the line is "suspiciously elliptical". Frankenberg took it as Antiochus IV's pagan rites (1 Maccabees 1:44-54); Gray thought the text robs that view of "much of its plausibility". The Plain English Translation follows the dative (see the variant) and gives the likely sense: he treated Jerusalem as pagans treat their cities and gods.
orig: καθὼς καὶ τὰ ἔθνη ἐν ταῖς πόλεσι τοὺς θεοὺς αὐτῶν (kathōs kai ta ethnē en tais polesi tous theous autōn)

a: the children of the covenant prevailed over them
p: The Greek verb epekratoun can mean "ruled them", "outdid them" or "joined them".
b: Gray says the sense of epekratoun autōn is uncertain: the Jews "surpassed" the Gentiles in wickedness (as 1:8 and 8:13 say), or "attached themselves" to them, though the Greek most naturally means "gained the mastery over them". The Plain English Translation says "prevailed over them", which leaves all three senses open; "outdid them" in wickedness fits the next line, where no one in Jerusalem did mercy and truth. "Children of the covenant" is a name for Israel; Peter tells the crowd, "You belong to the family of the prophets and of the covenant" (Acts 3:25).
orig: ἐπεκρατοῦσαν αὐτῶν υἱοὶ τῆς διαθήκης (epekratousan autōn huioi tēs diathēkēs)

a: Those who loved the assemblies of the devout
p: The devout fled to the deserts like sparrows. Their "assemblies" are gatherings of the faithful.
b: Synagōgai hosiōn, "the assemblies of the devout", are their gatherings for prayer and study; the word does not yet mean a synagogue building (compare 10:7). Flight to the desert recalls those in the days of Mattathias who "went down into the desert to settle there" (1 Maccabees 2:29). Ryle and James think the sparrow simile may come from Psalm 11:1, where the singer is told, "Fly off to your mountain, bird!" The psalm names no place of refuge.
orig: οἱ ἀγαπῶντες συναγωγὰς ὁσίων (hoi agapōntes synagōgas hosiōn)

a: those living abroad
p: Paroikia, "sojourning", here means the Jews living away from the land.
b: Gray explains that "the sojourning" (paroikia) is the Jews of the Dispersion, "temporary residents abroad", to whom it seemed a rare thing that any of the devout escaped alive from the faithless rulers of Jerusalem. Peter speaks of believers' "time as resident aliens" (paroikia, 1 Peter 1:17).
orig: ἐν ὀφθαλμοῖς παροικίας (en ophthalmois paroikias)

a: For the sky held back from dripping rain on the earth.
p: The poet ties a drought to the sins of Jerusalem's leaders, as Deuteronomy and Elijah's story do.
b: "Then the LORD's anger will blaze against you. He will shut up the sky, and there will be no rain" (Deuteronomy 11:17). Elijah's drought came on Ahab's sin (1 Kings 17:1). Gray suggests the argument is: "The disloyal sons of the covenant by their sins brought about a drought (cp. ii. 10), and this in turn caused the pious to wander far and wide."

a: The king was a law-breaker
p: King, judge and people all sinned. The line sums up the charge against the Hasmonean state.
b: The three offices are king, judge (the high priest and court) and people. The last Hasmoneans were both king and high priest, so "the king" and "the judge" may be one family. Hosea and Micah made the same sweeping charge (Hosea 4:1-9; Micah 3:9-11). Swete's note shows that the manuscript he calls i places 17:22 and the first half of 17:23 after the second half of 17:23.

a: the son of David
p: "Son of David" is the title Jesus is hailed by in the Gospels. Here it names the hoped-for king.
b: Huios Dauid here names the coming king of David's line. In the Gospels blind men call to Jesus, "Have mercy on us, Son of David!" (Matthew 9:27), the crowds shout "Hosanna to the Son of David!" (Matthew 21:9), and Jesus asks how the scribes can say "the Messiah is David's son" (Mark 12:35). Matthew opens with "Jesus Christ, son of David" (Matthew 1:1). The psalm prays that God will "raise up" this king, as God told David, "I will raise up your offspring to come after you" (2 Samuel 7:12). The site writes "son of David" lowercase here, as in Matthew 1:1.
orig: υἱὸν Δαυίδ (huion Dauid)
r: 2 Samuel 7:12; Matthew 1:1; Matthew 9:27; Matthew 21:9; Mark 12:35-37; Romans 1:3

a: at the time you have foreseen
p: The Greek is "the time which you saw". God knows the time; the psalm does not set a date.
b: Eis ton kairon hon ides sy, "at the time which you saw": Gray reports "knowest" from manuscripts H and V, and von Gebhardt's guess "chosest". Ryle and James link it with "the day he has chosen" in 18:6. Compare Jesus: "Knowing the times or the seasons does not belong to you" (Acts 1:7).
orig: εἰς τὸν καιρὸν ὃν ἴδες σύ (eis ton kairon hon ides sy)

a: Wrap strength around him like a belt
p: The king is girded with strength, as Isaiah's shoot of Jesse wears righteousness as a belt.
b: "He will wear righteousness as the band around his waist, and faithfulness as the band around his hips" (Isaiah 11:5). "God is the one who wraps me in strength" (Psalm 18:32). The prayer asks God to equip his king. The rest of the psalm shows that his strength is God's, not his army's (17:37-38).
orig: ὑπόζωσον αὐτὸν ἰσχὺν (hypozōson auton ischyn)

a: Clean Jerusalem of the nations
p: The king will purge Jerusalem of the Gentiles who trample it and drive out the sinners. A political, earthly hope.
b: This is the heart of the book's hope: a king who frees Jerusalem from foreign rule and from Jewish "sinners" (17:26). The "nations that trample" recall 2:2 and Pompey's soldiers. Jesus says "Jerusalem will be trampled by Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled" (Luke 21:24). The Jewish reading takes the hope at face value: a human king will do this. Christians have read it as a hope Jesus met in a way his hearers did not expect (Acts 1:6-8). See the chapter page.
orig: καθάρισον Ἰερουσαλὴμ ἀπὸ ἐθνῶν καταπατούντων (katharison Ierousalēm apo ethnōn katapatountōn)

a: with an iron rod
p: The potter's jars and the iron rod are Psalm 2:9. Revelation takes the same verse for Jesus.
b: "You will crush them with an iron rod; you will shatter them like a jar from the potter" (Psalm 2:9). The psalm uses the Greek wording of Psalm 2:9 (en rhabdō sidēra, skeuos kerameōs). Revelation applies the same verse to Jesus three times, using the Greek "shepherd" for "crush": he will "shepherd all the nations with an iron rod" (Revelation 12:5; compare Revelation 2:27; 19:15). Psalm 2 speaks of the LORD's "anointed one" (Psalm 2:2), the same title this psalm gives its king (17:36).
orig: ἐν ῥάβδῳ σιδηρᾷ (en rhabdō sidēra); ὡς σκεύη κεραμέως (hōs skeuē kerameōs)

a: by the word of his mouth
p: The king conquers by speaking, as Isaiah 11:4 says. Paul uses the line for Jesus' victory over the lawless one.
b: "His mouth will be a rod to strike the earth, and the breath of his lips will put the wicked to death" (Isaiah 11:4). The Greek of Isaiah has "he will strike the earth with the word of his mouth", the phrase used here and in 17:39. Paul: "The Lord Jesus will do away with him by the breath of his mouth" (2 Thessalonians 2:8), and Revelation's sword from the mouth (Revelation 19:15). In 4 Ezra 13 the Messiah destroys the nations with fire from his mouth.

a: He will bring together a holy people
t: The holy people and the tribes
p: The king gathers the scattered and judges the twelve tribes. Jesus promised the Twelve thrones to judge the tribes.
b: Israel was to be "a kingdom of priests, a holy nation" (Exodus 19:6). Ezekiel promised to gather the tribes and make them one under David (Ezekiel 37:21-24). Jesus told the Twelve: "you too will sit on twelve thrones and judge the twelve tribes of Israel" (Matthew 19:28), and Peter calls the church "a holy nation" (1 Peter 2:9). The site's note on Luke 22:30 cites this passage for the Jewish hope of the gathered tribes.

a: they are all their God's sons
p: The people of the restored kingdom are all "sons of God", as Hosea promised.
b: Hosea promised that Israel would be called "Children of the living God!" (Hosea 1:10). Israel as a whole is God's son (Exodus 4:22), and the king is God's son in Psalm 2:7. Here the title goes to every member of the purified people. Paul quotes Hosea for Jews and Gentiles in Christ (Romans 9:26) and says "you are all sons of God through faith" (Galatians 3:26).
orig: πάντες υἱοὶ θεοῦ (pantes huioi theou)

a: The resident alien and the foreigner will not settle among them again
p: Foreigners will no longer live among Israel. Ezekiel 47:22 gives them an inheritance; Isaiah welcomes them.
b: Joel promised that "outsiders will never pass through her again" (Joel 3:17), and Ryle and James cite it here. But other prophets open the land to foreigners: Ezekiel orders an inheritance for "the foreigners who live among you" (Ezekiel 47:22), and Isaiah calls the Temple "a house of prayer for all the peoples" (Isaiah 56:7). Ryle and James note that the nations are not destroyed here (17:31b, 17:34), only excluded from living in the land. The New Testament goes further, telling Gentile believers, "you are no longer strangers and resident aliens" (Ephesians 2:19). The psalm stands with Joel against Ezekiel 47 and Ephesians on this point.
orig: πάροικος καὶ ἀλλογενὴς (paroikos kai allogenēs)

a: Selah
p: The Greek is diapsalma, the Greek Psalms' word for selah. It occurs only twice in this book.
b: Diapsalma is the Septuagint's rendering of the Hebrew selah, a mark of unknown meaning in the Psalms, probably musical or liturgical (see the site's note at Psalm 3:2). It appears only here and at 18:10. Ryle and James note that the Moscow manuscript (Swete's m) omits it in both places and suspect that the man who wrote the headings added it, to make the book look more like the Davidic Psalter; if it is original, it points to use in worship.
orig: διάψαλμα (diapsalma)

a: he will give glory to the Lord in a place the whole earth can see
p: En episēmō means "in a conspicuous place" or "openly". Ryle and James saw raised Zion of Isaiah 2:2.
b: Ryle and James take episēmon in its usual sense, "conspicuous", and see an allusion to Isaiah 2:2, the mountain of the LORD's house "lifted higher than the hills". Gray reports Kittel's "openly before". The nations serving "under his yoke" come from Psalm 72:11, which in the Greek reads "all the nations will serve him".
orig: ἐν ἐπισήμῳ πάσης τῆς γῆς (en episēmō pasēs tēs gēs)

a: bringing as gifts her sons who had grown weak
p: The nations come to Jerusalem carrying Israel's exiles as gifts, as Isaiah 66:20 promised.
b: "They will bring all your brothers from all the nations as an offering to the LORD ... to my holy mountain, Jerusalem" (Isaiah 66:20). Ryle and James call the verse a condensing of Isaiah 66:18-20 and 60. "To see his glory" may be the king's glory or God's; 17:35 says "the glory of the Lord". Compare Isaiah 60:3: nations coming to Zion's light.

a: one whom God has taught
p: The king is didaktos hypo theou, "taught by God". Ryle and James see in this his "merely human nature".
b: Isaiah promised: "All your children will be the LORD's learners" (Isaiah 54:13), which Jesus quotes, "And all of them will be taught by God" (John 6:45). Ryle and James wrote that in this phrase "the merely human nature of the Messiah is here not obscurely indicated": he learns, as a wise king like Solomon learned (1 Kings 3:9-12). Gray suggests the Hebrew may have read simply "a righteous king taught of God", with "over them" a copyist's error.
orig: διδακτὸς ὑπὸ θεοῦ (didaktos hypo theou)

a: the Lord Messiah
p: Swete's Greek reads christos kyrios, "Messiah, Lord". Many scholars think the Hebrew meant "the LORD's anointed".
b: Christos translates Hebrew mashiach, "anointed one". In the Hebrew Bible "the LORD's anointed" (meshiach YHWH) is the reigning king (1 Samuel 24:6; Lamentations 4:20); in this psalm it is the coming son of David, so the site writes "Messiah". The manuscripts Swete printed read christos kyrios, two nominatives: "Messiah, Lord". Ryle and James list three views: (1) a correct rendering, with "lord" for the Hebrew adon, a title fit for a human king; (2) a mistranslation of "the LORD's anointed", as in the Greek of Lamentations 4:20, the view they credit to Ewald, Hilgenfeld, Geiger, Carrière, Vernes, Wellhausen, Robertson Smith and others; (3) a Christian change, which they reject. Gray adopts (2). The site's Luke 2:11 renders the same two words "Messiah and Lord". See the variant and the chapter page.
orig: χριστὸς κύριος (christos kyrios)
r: Lamentations 4:20; 1 Samuel 24:6; Psalm 2:2; Luke 2:11; Luke 2:26; Acts 2:36

a: horse and rider and bow
p: The king will not trust in horses or pile up gold, keeping Deuteronomy's law of the king that Solomon broke.
b: "He must not get himself many horses ... And he must not pile up great amounts of silver and gold for himself" (Deuteronomy 17:16-17). "These have chariots, and those have horses, but we call on the name of the LORD our God" (Psalm 20:7). Ryle and James saw here the contrast between the old Solomon, rich in horses and gold (1 Kings 10:26-29), and his coming "antitype". The last line is obscure; all manuscripts read "many" (pollois), and Ryle and James guessed ploiois, "by ships".
orig: ἐπὶ ἵππον καὶ ἀναβάτην καὶ τόξον (epi hippon kai anabatēn kai toxon)

a: The Lord himself is his King
p: The king's own King is the Lord. The line guards against any idea that the son of David replaces God.
b: Gray thinks the Greek may not reproduce the original closely and that the line contrasted trust in weapons with trust in God. Either way the poet keeps God above the king (compare 17:1, 17:51). "He will have mercy on all the nations" sounds generous; Gray thought the words corrupt, while Ryle and James rendered "He shall have mercy upon all the nations (that come) before him in fear". The nations here are spared, not destroyed (compare 17:31-34).

a: For he will shatter the earth
p: Swete prints kataxei, "he will shatter"; four manuscripts have pataxei, "he will strike", the word of Isaiah 11:4.
b: Kataxei is the future of katagnymi, "to break in pieces". Swete's note gives pataxei, "he will strike", from h, l, m, p and v, which is the verb of the Greek of Isaiah 11:4 ("he will strike the earth with the word of his mouth"). Gray renders "smite". Either way the king's weapon is his word (see 17:27 and the variant).
orig: κατάξει (kataxei)

a: He himself will be pure from sin
p: The king is "pure from sin". The psalm means a righteous man; Christians confess Jesus as sinless.
b: Katharos apo hamartias means clean from sin, fit to rule a holy people. Ryle and James read the whole picture of the king as human: taught by God, anointed, full of God's spirit, but with no word of "any superhuman origin". The New Testament says Jesus "has been tested in all things, in the same way we are, but apart from sin" (Hebrews 4:15; compare 1 Peter 2:22). The psalm and the New Testament agree that the true king is without sin; they differ on who he is.
orig: καὶ αὐτὸς καθαρὸς ἀπὸ ἁμαρτίας (kai autos katharos apo hamartias)

a: by a holy spirit
p: God makes the king strong by the holy spirit and wise in counsel: Isaiah 11:2 in other words.
b: "The LORD's Spirit will come to rest on him, a spirit of wisdom and understanding, a spirit of counsel and strength" (Isaiah 11:2). The Greek has en pneumati hagiō, "in holy spirit", with no article; a Jewish reader would hear God's own spirit, as in Psalm 51:11 and Isaiah 63:10-11. The Plain English Translation writes it lowercase and without "the", as the site's Isaiah 63:10-11 ("his holy spirit") and Wisdom 1:5 do; Gray has "by means of (His) holy spirit". Christian readers hear in it the Holy Spirit, who comes on Jesus at his baptism (Luke 3:22); Jesus reads Isaiah 61:1 of himself (Luke 4:18).
orig: δυνατὸν ἐν πνεύματι ἁγίῳ (dynaton en pneumati hagiō)
r: Isaiah 11:2; Isaiah 61:1; Isaiah 63:10-11; Psalm 51:11; Wisdom 1:5; Luke 3:22; Luke 4:18; 18:8

a: shepherding the Lord's flock
p: The son of David is a shepherd, as Ezekiel 34 promised: "my servant David" will shepherd them.
b: "I will set one shepherd over them, and he will shepherd them: my servant David" (Ezekiel 34:23). "Then he chose his servant David; he took him from the pens where the sheep were kept" (Psalm 78:70). Ryle and James call it "The King as shepherd of his people". Jesus says, "I am the good shepherd" (John 10:11). The Greek en pistei may mean "faithfully" or "in faith".

a: as equals
p: Swete prints isotēti, "in equality"; four manuscripts have hosiotēti, "in holiness".
b: Swete's note gives isotēti from the manuscripts he calls i, r and the margin of l, and hosiotēti, "in holiness", from h, the text of l, m, p and v; Gray agrees ("aright", literally "in equalness", so R J L margin; "in holiness", L text and H). Ryle and James printed "In holiness". "Equality" fits the next line: no one will lord it over another. See the variant.
orig: ἐν ἰσότητι (en isotēti)

a: fire-refined
p: The king's words are refined like gold. Psalm 12 says the LORD's sayings are silver refined seven times.
b: "The LORD's sayings are sayings without impurity, silver smelted in a crucible in the ground, refined seven times" (Psalm 12:6). The Greek of that psalm has the participle used here, pepyrōmena, "fire-tried". Psalm 19:10 calls God's rulings more desirable "than a mass of fine gold". The king's words have the quality of God's own word.
orig: πεπυρωμένα ὑπὲρ χρυσίον τὸ πρῶτον τίμιον (pepyrōmena hyper chrysion to prōton timion)

a: the words of holy ones
p: Gray takes "the holy ones" as the angels: the king speaks like the angels.
b: Gray takes "the holy ones" (hagioi) as the angels, comparing Psalm 89:5 ("the gathering of the holy ones") and Job 5:1. If so, the king speaks with the authority of God's heavenly court.
orig: ὡς λόγοι ἁγίων (hōs logoi hagiōn)

a: Happy are those who live in those days
p: The poets long to see the king's days. Jesus told his disciples their eyes were blessed to see them.
b: The same blessing returns in 18:7. Jesus said to his disciples, "How blessed are the eyes that are seeing what you see! For I tell you, many prophets and kings wanted to see what you are seeing, and they did not see it" (Luke 10:23-24; compare Matthew 13:16-17). The site's note on Luke 10:24 cites this book for the same longing. Neither text quotes the other; they share the hope.

a: the uncleanness of godless enemies
p: The enemies are "unclean" and "godless": the Gentile conquerors who defiled the Temple.
b: Bebēloi are the profane, those outside God's holiness; Pompey's soldiers had trampled the altar (2:2). The prayer ends where 17:1 began: "The Lord himself is our King." Zechariah's song asks for the same rescue: "salvation from our enemies, out of the grip of all who hate us" (Luke 1:71).
orig: ἀπὸ ἀκαθαρσίας ἐχθρῶν βεβήλων (apo akatharsias echthrōn bebēlōn)

a: Again, of the Lord's Messiah.
p: "Again, of the Lord's Messiah": the heading ties this psalm to Psalm 17. One group of manuscripts has "about" for "again".
b: Swete prints eti tou christou kyriou, "again, of the Lord's Messiah", with the manuscripts he calls i and r; h, l, p and v have epi, "about" (Gray: "Again of", R J; "upon", L H). The genitive christou kyriou is most naturally "of the Lord's Messiah", as in Luke 2:26, but it could also be the genitive of 17:36's "the Lord Messiah"; Ryle and James translate the heading "touching the Lord Messiah". See the variant.
orig: ἔτι τοῦ χριστοῦ κυρίου (eti tou christou kyriou)

a: Your eyes are watching over them
p: "Them" is the works of God's hands (18:1), not Israel.
b: Gray explains that "them" (auta, neuter) refers to "the works of your hands" in 18:1: God's eyes are on all his creation, and nothing in it lacks. Compare Psalm 145:15-16: "All eyes wait in hope for you ... You open your hand and fill every living thing with what it longs for."
orig: ἐπιβλέποντες ἐπ᾽ αὐτά (epiblepontes ep' auta)

a: a firstborn, an only son
p: Israel is God's firstborn (Exodus 4:22) and here his only son. 4 Ezra uses the same pair.
b: "Israel is my son, my firstborn" (Exodus 4:22). Ryle and James note that Hilgenfeld compared 4 Ezra 6:58, which calls Israel God's "firstborn, only-begotten". The Greek monogenēs, "only (son)", is John's word for Jesus (John 1:14; 3:16). Here it is Israel's title as God's one beloved people, and the point is discipline: God trains Israel as a father trains his only heir (13:8).
orig: ὡς υἱὸν πρωτότοκον μονογενῆ (hōs huion prōtotokon monogenē)

a: a willing soul
p: Swete's euēkoon is "ready to listen"; four manuscripts have hypēkoon, "obedient".
b: Swete's note gives euēkoon, "listening well", from i, l and r, and hypēkoon, "obedient", from h, m, p and v; the sense hardly changes. Ryle and James explain "from the folly that comes from not knowing" as the soul's lack of learning shown in its sins of ignorance (13:6).
orig: ψυχὴν εὐήκοον (psychēn euēkoon)

a: when he brings forward his Messiah
p: Anaxis means a bringing up or bringing back. Ryle and James rejected the idea that it implies a Messiah who already exists.
b: En anaxei christou autou. Ryle and James note that anaxis could mean "bringing again" or "bringing up", and that "bringing again" would suggest a Messiah existing before his appearing, an idea found in the Parables of Enoch (1 Enoch 48:3) and 4 Ezra. But since Psalms 17-18 describe the king fully as a man, they concluded that anaxis "is simply a rather more detailed equivalent" of "raise up" in 17:23. Gray agrees that the idea is very doubtful here. "His Messiah" is christou autou, God's anointed. "The day he has chosen" is literally "the day of choosing" (eklogē, as in 9:7).
orig: ἐν ἀνάξει χριστοῦ αὐτοῦ (en anaxei christou autou)

a: under the rod of discipline of the Lord's Messiah
p: Christou kyriou is "the Lord's Messiah", the phrase of Simeon's promise in Luke 2:26.
b: "He would not see death until his eyes had seen the Lord's Messiah" (Luke 2:26). The same Greek, christou kyriou, stands here. The "rod of discipline" is the shepherd-king's staff (17:26; Psalm 23:4); Ryle and James note that in 17:26 and 17:47 the Messiah wields it against Jew and Gentile alike. Wellhausen read the line as "in place of the rod of discipline comes the Lord's anointed" (taking a Hebrew tachat as "instead of"), which Ryle and James rejected and Gray reports.
orig: ὑπὸ ῥάβδον παιδείας χριστοῦ κυρίου (hypo rhabdon paideias christou kyriou)

a: in wisdom of spirit, of righteousness and of strength
p: The gifts of Isaiah 11:2 return: wisdom, spirit, strength.
b: The Greek order, "in wisdom of spirit and of righteousness and of strength", is awkward. Ryle and James say it must be translated as "in the spirit of wisdom", though they doubt the Greek ever read so. The source is Isaiah 11:2: "a spirit of wisdom and understanding, a spirit of counsel and strength" (compare 17:42).

a: before the Lord
t: Before the Lord, or in the Lord's fear?
p: Swete's text says "before the Lord"; most manuscripts say "in the fear of the Lord".
b: Swete prints enōpion kyriou, "before the Lord", with l and r; his note gives en phobō, "in the fear (of the Lord)", from h, m, p and v, which Ryle and James printed. The verbs are infinitives, Ryle and James argue: the coming king will guide each person, and so the whole people will come to fear God. See the variant.
orig: καταστῆσαι πάντας αὐτοὺς ἐνώπιον Κυρίου (katastēsai pantas autous enōpion Kyriou)

a: Selah
p: The second and last diapsalma in the book. After it the psalm changes subject.
b: On the Greek diapsalma see the note at 17:31. Ryle and James note that the Moscow manuscript (Swete's m) omits it here too, but punctuates as if the psalm ended at this word and begins the next verse with a capital. After this point the psalm turns to the stars, and Ryle and James printed 18:11-14 as a separate Psalm 19.
orig: διάψαλμα (diapsalma)

a: He set the lights in their courses
p: The sun, moon and stars keep the path God set them, a lesson in obedience for the people.
b: "Let lights appear in the sky's dome ... They will be signs, and will mark the appointed times, the days and the years" (Genesis 1:14). "He set a rule, and it will not be broken" (Psalm 148:6; compare Jeremiah 31:35). Ryle and James note how often Jewish writers dwelt on the order of the heavens. The lights walk "in the fear of God" (18:13), as the coming generation will (18:10). 1 Enoch's Astronomical Book makes the same point at length (1 Enoch 2:1; 72-82).

a: except when God commanded them by the order of his servants
p: The only exceptions are when God ordered them through his servants: Joshua's sun and Hezekiah's shadow.
b: The lights have never left their path "except when God commanded them by the order of his servants". This recalls Joshua's prayer, when "the sun stood in the middle of the sky" (Joshua 10:13), and Hezekiah's sign: "So the sun went back ten steps" (Isaiah 38:8). The poem ends abruptly, with no closing blessing; Gray thinks "the conclusion of the Psalm has been lost", and with Ryle and James that 18:11-14 was "perhaps originally a distinct Psalm".
